source_sentence: The applications of biotechnology include therapeutics, diagnostics, genetically modified crops for agriculture, processed food, bioremediation, waste treatment, and energy production.
question: Which of the following is NOT listed as an application of biotechnology in NCERT Class 12 Biology?

options.A: Therapeutics and diagnostics

explanation: Biotechnology applications include therapeutics, diagnostics, GM crops, processed food, bioremediation, waste treatment, and energy production—not fossil fuel mining.

source_sentence: Three critical research areas of biotechnology are: (i) Providing the best catalyst in the form of improved organism usually a microbe or pure enzyme.
question: One of the three critical research areas of biotechnology is providing the best catalyst in the form of:

options.A: Improved organism, usually a microbe or pure enzyme

explanation: A critical research area is providing the best catalyst, usually an improved microbe or pure enzyme.

source_sentence: (ii) Creating optimal conditions through engineering for a catalyst to act.
question: Which critical research area of biotechnology involves creating optimal conditions through engineering for a catalyst to act?

options.A: Downstream processing

explanation: Creating optimal engineered conditions for a catalyst to act is one of the three critical biotechnology research areas.

source_sentence: (iii) Downstream processing technologies to purify the protein/organic compound.
question: Downstream processing technologies in biotechnology are used to:

options.A: Purify the protein or organic compound

explanation: Downstream processing technologies purify the protein or organic compound produced by biotechnological processes.

source_sentence: Let us take a look at the three options that can be thought for increasing food production (i) agro-chemical based agriculture; (ii) organic agriculture; and (iii) genetically engineered crop-based agriculture.
question: Which of the following is one of the three options considered for increasing food production?

options.A: Genetically engineered crop-based agriculture

explanation: The three options are agro-chemical based agriculture, organic agriculture, and genetically engineered crop-based agriculture.

source_sentence: The Green Revolution succeeded in tripling the food supply but yet it was not enough to feed the growing human population.
question: Regarding the Green Revolution, the chapter states that it:

options.A: Failed to increase food supply at all
options.B: Tripled the food supply but was still insufficient for the growing population
options.C: Eliminated the need for pesticides entirely
options.D: Made agrochemicals affordable for all developing-world farmers

explanation: The Green Revolution tripled food supply but was not enough to feed the growing human population.

source_sentence: Increased yields have partly been due to the use of improved crop varieties, but mainly due to the use of better management practices and use of agrochemicals (fertilisers and pesticides).
question: Increased crop yields during the Green Revolution were mainly due to:

options.A: Better management practices and use of agrochemicals
options.B: Complete replacement of crops with GM varieties only
options.C: Elimination of all fertilizers and pesticides
options.D: Exclusive use of organic farming methods

explanation: Yields increased partly from improved varieties but mainly from better management and agrochemical use.

source_sentence: However, for farmers in the developing world, agrochemicals are often too expensive, and further increases in yield with existing varieties are not possible using conventional breeding.
question: Why is conventional breeding alone insufficient for further yield increases in developing countries?

options.A: Agrochemicals are often too expensive and conventional breeding cannot further improve existing varieties sufficiently
options.B: Conventional breeding has no role in crop improvement
options.C: All developing countries have banned agrochemicals
options.D: Existing crop varieties have unlimited yield potential through breeding alone

explanation: Agrochemicals are costly for developing-world farmers, and conventional breeding cannot achieve further sufficient yield gains with existing varieties.

source_sentence: As traditional breeding techniques failed to keep pace with demand and to provide sufficiently fast and efficient systems for crop improvement, another technology called tissue culture got developed.
question: Tissue culture technology was developed because:

options.A: Traditional breeding could not keep pace with demand for fast, efficient crop improvement
options.B: All plants naturally resist tissue culture
options.D: Micropropagation was discovered in ancient times

explanation: Tissue culture emerged when traditional breeding failed to provide sufficiently fast and efficient crop improvement systems.

source_sentence: It was learnt by scientists, during 1950s, that whole plants could be regenerated from explants, i.e., any part of a plant taken out and grown in a test tube, under sterile conditions in special nutrient media.
question: An explant in plant tissue culture refers to:

options.A: Any part of a plant taken out and grown in vitro under sterile conditions
options.B: Only the root tip of a seedling
options.D: A whole plant grown only in soil

explanation: An explant is any plant part removed and cultured in a test tube under sterile conditions in nutrient media.

source_sentence: This capacity to generate a whole plant from any cell/explant is called totipotency.
question: The ability of a plant cell or explant to regenerate into a whole plant is called:

options.A: Totipotency

explanation: Totipotency is the capacity to generate a whole plant from any cell or explant.

source_sentence: The nutrient medium must provide a carbon source such as sucrose and also inorganic salts, vitamins, amino acids and growth regulators like auxins, cytokines etc.
question: Which of the following must be provided in the nutrient medium for in vitro propagation of plant explants?

options.A: Sucrose, inorganic salts, vitamins, amino acids, and growth regulators

explanation: The medium must supply a carbon source (sucrose), inorganic salts, vitamins, amino acids, and growth regulators like auxins and cytokinins.

source_sentence: This method of producing thousands of plants through tissue culture is called micro-propagation.
question: The production of thousands of plants through tissue culture is called:

options.A: Micro-propagation

explanation: Micro-propagation is the tissue culture method used to produce thousands of plants in short durations.

source_sentence: Each of these plants will be genetically identical to the original plant from which they were grown, i.e., they are somaclones.
question: Plants produced by micro-propagation that are genetically identical to the original plant are called:

options.A: Somaclones

explanation: Micro-propagated plants genetically identical to the parent are termed somaclones.

source_sentence: Many important food plants like tomato, banana, apple, etc., have been produced on commercial scale using this method.
question: Which food plants have been commercially produced using micro-propagation according to the chapter?

options.A: Tomato, banana, and apple

explanation: Tomato, banana, apple, and other important food plants have been commercially micro-propagated.

source_sentence: Even if the plant is infected with a virus, the meristem (apical and axillary) is free of virus.
question: Why is the meristem used to obtain virus-free plants from infected plants?

options.A: Meristem (apical and axillary) is free of virus even when the rest of the plant is infected
options.B: Meristem contains the highest concentration of virus
options.C: Meristem cannot be cultured in vitro
options.D: Viruses infect only root tissues, not shoots

explanation: Apical and axillary meristems are virus-free even in infected plants, allowing recovery of healthy plants through in vitro culture.

source_sentence: Scientists have succeeded in culturing meristems of banana, sugarcane, potato, etc.
question: Meristem culture for virus-free plants has succeeded in:

options.A: Banana, sugarcane, and potato

explanation: Meristems of banana, sugarcane, potato, and other plants have been successfully cultured to obtain virus-free plants.

source_sentence: Isolated protoplasts from two different varieties of plants – each having a desirable character – can be fused to get hybrid protoplasts, which can be further grown to form a new plant.
question: Somatic hybridisation involves:

options.A: Fusion of protoplasts from two plant varieties followed by regeneration of a new plant
options.B: Cross-pollination between two flowering plants in the field only
options.C: Introduction of Bt toxin gene into cotton
options.D: Production of insulin in E. coli

explanation: Somatic hybridisation fuses isolated protoplasts from two varieties, each with a desirable trait, to form a new hybrid plant.

source_sentence: These hybrids are called somatic hybrids while the process is called somatic hybridisation.
question: Hybrids produced by fusion of plant protoplasts are called:

options.A: Somatic hybrids

explanation: Plants from fused protoplasts are somatic hybrids; the process is somatic hybridisation.

source_sentence: Plants, bacteria, fungi and animals whose genes have been altered by manipulation are called Genetically Modified Organisms (GMO).
question: Genetically Modified Organisms (GMOs) are:

options.A: Plants, bacteria, fungi, or animals whose genes have been altered by manipulation
options.C: Organisms produced solely by conventional breeding without gene manipulation

explanation: GMOs are plants, bacteria, fungi, or animals whose genes have been deliberately altered through genetic manipulation.

source_sentence: Genetic modification has: (i) made crops more tolerant to abiotic stresses (cold, drought, salt, heat).
question: One benefit of genetic modification of crops is:

options.A: Increased tolerance to abiotic stresses like cold, drought, salt, and heat
options.B: Complete elimination of all plant diseases
options.C: Removal of all nutritional content from food

explanation: GM crops can be made more tolerant to abiotic stresses including cold, drought, salt, and heat.

source_sentence: (ii) reduced reliance on chemical pesticides (pest-resistant crops).
question: Pest-resistant GM crops help to:

options.A: Reduce reliance on chemical pesticides

explanation: Pest-resistant GM crops reduce dependence on chemical pesticides.

source_sentence: (iii) helped to reduce post harvest losses.
question: Genetic modification of crops can help to:

options.A: Reduce post-harvest losses
options.C: Eliminate the need for any storage

explanation: GM crops can help reduce losses after harvest.

source_sentence: Some strains of Bacillus thuringiensis produce proteins that kill certain insects such as lepidopterans (tobacco budworm, armyworm), coleopterans (beetles) and dipterans (flies, mosquitoes).
question: Bt proteins from Bacillus thuringiensis can kill insects belonging to which groups?

options.A: Lepidopterans, coleopterans, and dipterans

explanation: Some Bt strains produce proteins lethal to lepidopterans, coleopterans, and dipterans.

source_sentence: B. thuringiensis forms protein crystals during a particular phase of their growth. These crystals contain a toxic insecticidal protein.
question: During a particular growth phase, Bacillus thuringiensis forms:

options.A: Protein crystals containing toxic insecticidal protein

explanation: B. thuringiensis produces protein crystals containing insecticidal toxin during a specific growth phase.

source_sentence: Actually, the Bt toxin protein exist as inactive protoxins but once an insect ingests the inactive toxin, it is converted into an active form of toxin due to the alkaline pH of the gut which solubilizes the crystals.
question: Crystals of Bt toxin produced by some bacteria do not kill the bacteria themselves because:

options.A: The toxin exists as inactive protoxin
options.B: Bacteria are resistant to all proteins
options.C: The toxin is always in active form inside bacteria
options.D: Bacteria enclose toxin in a special sac that insects digest

explanation: Bt toxin exists as inactive protoxin in bacteria; it becomes active only after ingestion and alkaline solubilisation in the insect gut.

source_sentence: The activated toxin binds to the surface of midgut epithelial cells and creates pores that cause cell swelling and lysis and eventually cause death of the insect.
question: How does activated Bt toxin kill insects?

options.A: It binds midgut epithelial cells, forms pores, causes swelling and lysis leading to death
options.B: It blocks photosynthesis in plant leaves
options.D: It prevents insulin secretion in insects

explanation: Activated Bt toxin binds midgut epithelial cells, creates pores, and causes cell swelling, lysis, and insect death.

source_sentence: (iv) increased efficiency of mineral usage by plants (this prevents early exhaustion of fertility of soil).
question: GM crops with increased efficiency of mineral usage help to:

options.A: Prevent early exhaustion of soil fertility

explanation: More efficient mineral use by GM plants helps prevent premature depletion of soil fertility.

source_sentence: (v) enhanced nutritional value of food, e.g., golden rice, i.e., Vitamin 'A' enriched rice.
question: Golden rice is an example of GM crop with:

options.A: Enhanced nutritional value — Vitamin A enriched rice
options.B: Resistance to all bacterial diseases only
options.C: Production of human insulin in grains

explanation: Golden rice is Vitamin A-enriched rice, illustrating enhanced nutritional value through genetic modification.

source_sentence: Bt toxin is produced by a bacterium called Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt for short). Bt toxin gene has been cloned from the bacteria and been expressed in plants to provide resistance to insects without the need for insecticides; in effect created a bio-pesticide.
question: Expression of the Bt toxin gene in crop plants creates:

options.A: Insect resistance without need for insecticides — a bio-pesticide
options.D: Production of human growth hormone in leaves

explanation: Cloning and expressing the Bt toxin gene in plants provides insect resistance and acts as a bio-pesticide.

source_sentence: Examples are Bt cotton, Bt corn, rice, tomato, potato and soyabean etc.
question: Which of the following is an example of a Bt crop mentioned in the chapter?

options.A: Bt cotton

explanation: Bt cotton, Bt corn, rice, tomato, potato, and soybean are examples of Bt crops.

source_sentence: The choice of genes depends upon the crop and the targeted pest, as most Bt toxins are insect-group specific.
question: Why is the choice of Bt toxin gene specific for each crop and pest?

options.A: Most Bt toxins are insect-group specific
options.B: All Bt toxins kill every organism equally
options.D: Bt toxins work only in bacteria, not plants

explanation: Bt toxin genes are selected based on crop and target pest because most Bt toxins are specific to particular insect groups.

source_sentence: The proteins encoded by the genes cryIAc and cryIIAb control the cotton bollworms, that of cryIAb controls corn borer.
question: Which Cry proteins control cotton bollworms?

options.A: CryIAc and CryIIAb

explanation: CryIAc and CryIIAb proteins control cotton bollworms; CryIAb controls corn borer.

source_sentence: A nematode Meloidegyne incognitia infects the roots of tobacco plants and causes a great reduction in yield.
question: Meloidegyne incognitia is a nematode that:

options.A: Infects tobacco roots and greatly reduces yield
options.C: Is used to make human insulin
options.D: Is a transgenic cow producing alpha-lactalbumin

explanation: Meloidegyne incognitia parasitises tobacco roots and causes significant yield reduction.

source_sentence: RNAi takes place in all eukaryotic organisms as a method of cellular defense.
question: RNA interference (RNAi) occurs in:

options.A: All eukaryotic organisms as a cellular defense method

explanation: RNAi is a method of cellular defense present in all eukaryotic organisms.

source_sentence: This method involves silencing of a specific mRNA due to a complementary dsRNA molecule that binds to and prevents translation of the mRNA (silencing).
question: RNA interference silences a specific mRNA by:

options.A: Complementary dsRNA binding and preventing translation
options.B: Directly deleting the gene from chromosomes
options.C: Increasing transcription of the target gene

explanation: RNAi uses complementary dsRNA that binds target mRNA and prevents its translation, thereby silencing it.

source_sentence: Using Agrobacterium vectors, nematode-specific genes were introduced into the host plant.
question: In the nematode resistance strategy for tobacco, genes were introduced into the host plant using:

options.A: Agrobacterium vectors

explanation: Nematode-specific genes were introduced into the host plant using Agrobacterium vectors.

source_sentence: The introduction of DNA was such that it produced both sense and anti-sense RNA in the host cells. These two RNA's being complementary to each other formed a double stranded (dsRNA) that initiated RNAi.
question: How was dsRNA formed in transgenic plants for nematode resistance?

options.A: Sense and anti-sense RNA transcribed from introduced DNA formed complementary dsRNA
options.B: Bt toxin crystals were sprayed on roots
options.D: Protoplasts of tobacco and potato were fused

explanation: Introduced DNA produced sense and anti-sense RNA that paired to form dsRNA, triggering RNAi.

source_sentence: The consequence was that the parasite could not survive in a transgenic host expressing specific interfering RNA. The transgenic plant therefore got itself protected from the parasite.
question: The outcome of RNAi-based nematode resistance in transgenic tobacco is that:

options.A: The nematode parasite cannot survive in the transgenic host
options.B: The plant becomes more susceptible to nematodes
options.C: The nematode produces more Bt toxin

explanation: Silencing nematode-specific mRNA prevents parasite survival, protecting the transgenic plant.

source_sentence: The recombinant DNA technological processes have made immense impact in the area of healthcare by enabling mass production of safe and more effective therapeutic drugs.
question: Recombinant DNA technology has impacted healthcare mainly by enabling:

options.A: Mass production of safe and more effective therapeutic drugs
options.C: Exclusive use of animal-derived insulin only
options.D: Ban on all genetic engineering in medicine

explanation: rDNA technology enables large-scale production of safer, more effective therapeutic drugs.

source_sentence: Further, the recombinant therapeutics do not induce unwanted immunological responses as is common in case of similar products isolated from non-human sources.
question: Recombinant therapeutics are preferred over products from non-human sources because they:

options.A: Do not induce unwanted immunological responses as commonly seen with non-human products
options.C: Are structurally unrelated to human proteins

explanation: Recombinant therapeutics match human proteins and avoid the immunological reactions common with non-human isolates.

source_sentence: At present, about 30 recombinant therapeutics have been approved for human-use the world over. In India, 12 of these are presently being marketed.
question: Approximately how many recombinant therapeutics are approved worldwide, and how many are marketed in India?

options.A: About 30 worldwide; 12 in India

explanation: About 30 recombinant therapeutics are approved globally; 12 are marketed in India.

source_sentence: Insulin used for diabetes was earlier extracted from pancreas of slaughtered cattle and pigs.
question: Before recombinant DNA technology, insulin for diabetes was obtained from:

options.A: Pancreas of slaughtered cattle and pigs

explanation: Insulin was earlier extracted from the pancreas of slaughtered cattle and pigs.

source_sentence: Insulin from an animal source, though caused some patients to develop allergy or other types of reactions to the foreign protein.
question: A problem with animal-derived insulin was that:

options.A: Some patients developed allergy or reactions to the foreign protein
options.B: It was identical to human insulin in all patients
options.C: It could never be administered by injection

explanation: Animal insulin, being a foreign protein, caused allergies and other reactions in some patients.

source_sentence: Insulin consists of two short polypeptide chains: chain A and chain B, that are linked together by disulphide bridges.
question: Mature human insulin consists of:

options.A: Chains A and B linked by disulphide bridges
options.B: A single polypeptide with no disulphide bonds
options.D: Three chains named X, Y, and Z

explanation: Insulin has two short polypeptide chains, A and B, connected by disulphide bridges.

source_sentence: In mammals, including humans, insulin is synthesised as a pro-hormone which contains an extra stretch called the C peptide.
question: In mammals, insulin is initially synthesised as:

options.A: A pro-hormone containing an extra C peptide stretch
options.B: Mature insulin with only A and B chains from the start

explanation: Insulin is made first as a pro-hormone that includes an extra C peptide region.

source_sentence: This C peptide is not present in the mature insulin and is removed during maturation into insulin.
question: Regarding the C peptide in insulin biosynthesis:

options.A: It is removed during maturation and is absent from mature insulin
options.B: It remains permanently in functional insulin
options.C: It replaces chain B in mature insulin
options.D: It is added after insulin is secreted

explanation: The C peptide is cleaved off during maturation and is not present in functional insulin.

source_sentence: In 1983, Eli Lilly an American company prepared two DNA sequences corresponding to A and B, chains of human insulin and introduced them in plasmids of E. coli to produce insulin chains.
question: In 1983, Eli Lilly produced human insulin chains by:

options.A: Introducing DNA sequences for A and B chains into E. coli plasmids
options.B: Extracting insulin only from pig pancreas

explanation: Eli Lilly cloned A and B chain DNA sequences into E. coli plasmids to produce insulin chains.

source_sentence: Chains A and B were produced separately, extracted and combined by creating disulfide bonds to form human insulin.
question: How was mature human insulin obtained from recombinant A and B chains?

options.A: Chains were produced separately and combined by creating disulphide bonds
options.B: Chains were orally administered to patients directly
options.C: C peptide was permanently fused to chain A
options.D: Chains were obtained only from Rosie the transgenic cow

explanation: A and B chains were made separately in E. coli, then joined by disulphide bonds to form insulin.

source_sentence: Gene therapy is a collection of methods that allows correction of a gene defect that has been diagnosed in a child/embryo.
question: Gene therapy is best defined as:

options.A: Methods to correct a diagnosed gene defect by inserting genes into cells and tissues
options.B: Use of chemical pesticides on GM crops
options.C: Production of somaclones through tissue culture

explanation: Gene therapy corrects diagnosed genetic defects by delivering functional genes into a patient's cells and tissues.

source_sentence: Correction of a genetic defect involves delivery of a normal gene into the individual or embryo to take over the function of and compensate for the non-functional gene.
question: Correction of a genetic defect through gene therapy involves:

options.A: Delivering a normal gene to compensate for a non-functional gene
options.B: Removing all chromosomes from the patient
options.C: Silencing all mRNA in the body
options.D: Spraying Bt toxin on affected tissues

explanation: A normal gene is delivered to take over the function of the defective gene.

source_sentence: The first clinical gene therapy was given in 1990 to a 4-year old girl with adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency.
question: The first clinical gene therapy (1990) was administered to a child with:

options.A: Adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency

explanation: The first clinical gene therapy in 1990 treated a 4-year-old girl with ADA deficiency.

source_sentence: This enzyme is crucial for the immune system to function. The disorder is caused due to the deletion of the gene for adenosine deaminase.
question: ADA deficiency affects the immune system because:

options.A: Adenosine deaminase enzyme is crucial for immune function and its gene is deleted in the disorder
options.B: ADA enzyme digests Bt toxin in the gut
options.C: ADA is the C peptide of insulin

explanation: ADA is essential for immune function; the disorder results from deletion of the ADA gene.

source_sentence: In some children ADA deficiency can be cured by bone marrow transplantation; in others it can be treated by enzyme replacement therapy, in which functional ADA is given to the patient by injection.
question: Conventional treatments for ADA deficiency include:

options.A: Bone marrow transplantation and enzyme replacement therapy by injection

explanation: ADA deficiency may be treated by bone marrow transplant or enzyme replacement with injected functional ADA.

source_sentence: But the problem with both of these approaches that they are not completely curative.
question: Bone marrow transplantation and enzyme replacement therapy for ADA deficiency are:

options.A: Not completely curative
options.B: Always permanently curative in every case
options.D: Preferred over all forms of gene therapy in every case without limitation

explanation: Neither bone marrow transplant nor enzyme replacement is completely curative for ADA deficiency.

source_sentence: A functional ADA cDNA (using a retroviral vector) is then introduced into these lymphocytes, which are subsequently returned to the patient.
question: In ADA gene therapy, functional ADA cDNA is introduced into lymphocytes using:

options.A: A retroviral vector

explanation: Functional ADA cDNA is delivered into cultured lymphocytes via a retroviral vector before returning them to the patient.

source_sentence: However, as these cells are not immortal, the patient requires periodic infusion of such genetically engineered lymphocytes.
question: Why do ADA gene therapy patients need periodic infusion of engineered lymphocytes?

options.A: The lymphocytes are not immortal and must be replenished
options.B: Retroviral vectors destroy all red blood cells immediately
options.D: Lymphocytes cannot be grown in culture

explanation: Engineered lymphocytes are not immortal, so patients need repeated infusions.

source_sentence: However, if the gene isolate from marrow cells producing ADA is introduced into cells at early embryonic stages, it could be a permanent cure.
question: A potentially permanent cure for ADA deficiency would involve:

options.A: Introducing the ADA gene into cells at early embryonic stages

explanation: Introducing the ADA gene at early embryonic stages could provide a permanent cure.

source_sentence: Recombinant DNA technology, Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) and Enzyme Linked Immuno-sorbent Assay (ELISA) are some of the techniques that serve the purpose of early diagnosis.
question: Techniques used for early molecular diagnosis include:

options.A: rDNA technology, PCR, and ELISA

explanation: Early diagnosis uses rDNA technology, PCR, and ELISA among other molecular methods.

source_sentence: However, very low concentration of a bacteria or virus (at a time when the symptoms of the disease are not yet visible) can be detected by amplification of their nucleic acid by PCR.
question: PCR allows early detection of pathogens because it:

options.A: Amplifies nucleic acids even when pathogen concentration is very low and symptoms are absent
options.B: Works only after symptoms are severe
options.C: Detects only antibodies, never nucleic acids
options.D: Can be used only for plant nematodes

explanation: PCR amplifies pathogen nucleic acids, enabling detection before visible symptoms when concentrations are very low.

source_sentence: PCR is now routinely used to detect HIV in suspected AIDS patients.
question: PCR is routinely used to detect:

options.A: HIV in suspected AIDS patients
options.B: Only vitamin content in golden rice
options.C: Only Bt toxin crystals in bacteria
options.D: Only patent status of Basmati rice

explanation: PCR is routinely employed to detect HIV in suspected AIDS cases.

source_sentence: It is being used to detect mutations in genes in suspected cancer patients too.
question: Besides HIV detection, PCR is also used to:

options.A: Detect gene mutations in suspected cancer patients

explanation: PCR helps detect mutations in genes of suspected cancer patients.

source_sentence: A single stranded DNA or RNA, tagged with a radioactive molecule (probe) is allowed to hybridise to its complementary DNA in a clone of cells followed by detection using autoradiography.
question: In probe-based mutation detection, a radioactive single-stranded DNA or RNA probe:

options.A: Hybridises to complementary DNA and is detected by autoradiography
options.B: Digests all mRNA in the cell
options.C: Produces Bt toxin in midgut cells

explanation: A labelled probe hybridises to complementary DNA; autoradiography reveals which clones carry the target sequence.

source_sentence: The clone having the mutated gene will hence not appear on the photographic film, because the probe will not have complementarity with the mutated gene.
question: In autoradiography-based gene detection, a clone with a mutated gene:

options.A: Will not appear on the film because the probe lacks complementarity with the mutation
options.B: Will show the brightest signal on the film
options.C: Cannot exist in any cell culture

explanation: Mutated sequences fail to hybridise with the normal probe and therefore do not show on autoradiography.

source_sentence: ELISA is based on the principle of antigen-antibody interaction.
question: ELISA is based on the principle of:

options.A: Antigen-antibody interaction

explanation: ELISA detects infections using specific antigen-antibody interactions.

source_sentence: Infection by pathogen can be detected by the presence of antigens (proteins, glycoproteins, etc.) or by detecting the antibodies synthesised against the pathogen.
question: ELISA can detect infection by identifying:

options.A: Pathogen antigens or antibodies produced against the pathogen
options.D: Only Cry gene sequences in cotton

explanation: ELISA detects either pathogen antigens or host antibodies against the pathogen.

source_sentence: Animals that have had their DNA manipulated to possess and express an extra (foreign) gene are known as transgenic animals.
question: Transgenic animals are those that:

options.A: Have manipulated DNA to possess and express an extra foreign gene
options.B: Are produced only by natural mating without any DNA manipulation
options.C: Are identical somaclones from tissue culture
options.D: Are bacteria producing only Bt toxin

explanation: Transgenic animals carry and express an introduced foreign gene in their manipulated DNA.

source_sentence: Transgenic rats, rabbits, pigs, sheep, cows and fish have been produced, although over 95 per cent of all existing transgenic animals are mice.
question: Which statement about transgenic animals is correct?

options.A: Over 95% of existing transgenic animals are mice, though rats, rabbits, pigs, sheep, cows, and fish have also been produced
options.B: Only fish have been made transgenic
options.D: Transgenic animals cannot include cows or sheep

explanation: Many species are transgenic, but over 95% of all transgenic animals are mice.

source_sentence: Transgenic animals can be specifically designed to allow the study of how genes are regulated, and how they affect the normal functions of the body and its development.
question: One reason for producing transgenic animals is to:

options.A: Study gene regulation and effects on normal body functions and development
options.B: Eliminate all ethical concerns about biotechnology

explanation: Transgenic animals help study how genes are regulated and how they influence development and physiology.

source_sentence: Many transgenic animals are designed to increase our understanding of how genes contribute to the development of disease. These are specially made to serve as models for human diseases.
question: Transgenic animal models of human disease are created to:

options.A: Increase understanding of how genes contribute to disease and enable investigation of new treatments
options.C: Replace PCR in all diagnostic labs
options.D: Eliminate the need for any vaccines

explanation: Disease-model transgenic animals help study genetic contributions to disease and test new treatments.

source_sentence: Today transgenic models exist for many human diseases such as cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis and Alzheimer's.
question: Transgenic models exist for human diseases including:

options.A: Cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis, and Alzheimer's
options.C: Only vitamin A deficiency in rice

explanation: Transgenic models are available for cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis, Alzheimer's, and other diseases.

source_sentence: Transgenic animals that produce useful biological products can be created by the introduction of the portion of DNA (or genes) which codes for a particular product such as human protein (α-1-antitrypsin) used to treat emphysema.
question: Transgenic animals can be engineered to produce biological products such as:

options.A: Human α-1-antitrypsin used to treat emphysema
options.B: Bt toxin crystals for insect midgut pores only in plants
options.C: Only somatic hybrid seeds of tomato-potato

explanation: Transgenic animals can express human proteins like α-1-antitrypsin for treating emphysema.

source_sentence: Similar attempts are being made for treatment of phenylketonuria (PKU) and cystic fibrosis.
question: Besides emphysema, transgenic animal research for biological products includes efforts for:

options.A: Phenylketonuria (PKU) and cystic fibrosis

explanation: Similar transgenic approaches are being developed for PKU and cystic fibrosis treatments.

source_sentence: In 1997, the first transgenic cow, Rosie, produced human protein-enriched milk (2.4 grams per litre). The milk contained the human alpha-lactalbumin and was nutritionally a more balanced product for human babies than natural cow-milk.
question: Rosie, the first transgenic cow (1997), produced milk containing:

options.A: Human alpha-lactalbumin — 2.4 g/L — nutritionally more balanced for human babies
options.B: Bt CryIAc protein for pest control

explanation: Rosie produced milk with 2.4 g/L human alpha-lactalbumin, better suited nutritionally for human infants.

source_sentence: Transgenic mice are being developed for use in testing the safety of vaccines before they are used on humans.
question: Transgenic mice are being developed to:

options.A: Test vaccine safety before human use
options.B: Replace all insulin production in bacteria

explanation: Transgenic mice are used to evaluate vaccine safety prior to human administration.

source_sentence: Transgenic mice are being used to test the safety of the polio vaccine. If successful and found to be reliable, they could replace the use of monkeys to test the safety of batches of the vaccine.
question: Successful use of transgenic mice for polio vaccine safety testing could:

options.A: Replace monkeys for testing vaccine batch safety
options.B: Eliminate the need for any vaccines

explanation: Reliable transgenic mouse testing could replace monkeys in polio vaccine safety testing.

source_sentence: Transgenic animals are made that carry genes which make them more sensitive to toxic substances than non-transgenic animals. They are then exposed to the toxic substances and the effects studied.
question: In chemical safety testing, transgenic animals are modified to be:

options.A: More sensitive to toxic substances than non-transgenic animals
options.C: Unable to express any foreign genes

explanation: Toxicity testing uses transgenic animals made hypersensitive to toxic substances for faster, detectable responses.

source_sentence: Toxicity testing in such animals will allow us to obtain results in less time.
question: An advantage of toxicity testing using sensitive transgenic animals is:

options.A: Results can be obtained in less time
options.D: PCR is no longer required for diagnosis

explanation: Hypersensitive transgenic animals yield toxicity test results more quickly.

source_sentence: The manipulation of living organisms by the human race cannot go on any further, without regulation.
question: According to the chapter, manipulation of living organisms requires:

options.A: Regulation and ethical standards
options.B: Complete absence of any government oversight

explanation: The text emphasises that continued manipulation of living organisms must be regulated.

source_sentence: Genetic modification of organisms can have unpredictable results when such organisms are introduced into the ecosystem.
question: A biological concern about releasing genetically modified organisms into ecosystems is that:

options.A: Effects can be unpredictable
options.B: GM organisms always remain confined to laboratories
options.C: Ecosystems cannot be affected by any organism
options.D: All GM organisms instantly die outside labs

explanation: Introducing GMOs into ecosystems may have unpredictable biological consequences.

source_sentence: Therefore, the Indian Government has set up organisations such as GEAC (Genetic Engineering Approval Committee), which will make decisions regarding the validity of GM research and the safety of introducing GM-organisms for public services.
question: GEAC (Genetic Engineering Approval Committee) in India is responsible for:

options.A: Decisions on validity of GM research and safety of introducing GM organisms for public services
options.B: Mass production of insulin in patients' homes
options.C: Micropropagation of all food plants commercially
options.D: Issuing patents on Basmati rice in the USA

explanation: GEAC evaluates GM research validity and safety before GM organisms are introduced for public services.

source_sentence: There is growing public anger that certain companies are being granted patents for products and technologies that make use of the genetic materials, plants and other biological resources that have long been identified, developed and used by farmers and indigenous people of a specific region/country.
question: Public anger over patents in biotechnology relates to:

options.A: Companies patenting genetic materials and bio-resources long used by farmers and indigenous people
options.B: Free sharing of all GM crop technologies without restriction
options.C: Ban on all recombinant therapeutics in India
options.D: Mandatory use of only animal insulin

explanation: Concern arises when patents are granted on biological resources traditionally developed and used by local communities.

source_sentence: There are an estimated 200,000 varieties of rice in India alone.
question: Approximately how many varieties of rice exist in India according to the chapter?

options.A: About 200,000

explanation: India alone has an estimated 200,000 rice varieties, reflecting rich biodiversity.

source_sentence: Basmati rice is distinct for its unique aroma and flavour and 27 documented varieties of Basmati are grown in India.
question: How many documented varieties of Basmati rice are grown in India?
explanation: India grows 27 documented Basmati varieties known for unique aroma and flavour.

source_sentence: In 1997, an American company got patent rights on Basmati rice through the US Patent and Trademark Office.
question: In 1997, an American company obtained patent rights on Basmati rice through:

options.A: The US Patent and Trademark Office

explanation: In 1997 a US company secured Basmati-related patent rights via the US Patent and Trademark Office.

source_sentence: Indian Basmati was crossed with semi-dwarf varieties and claimed as an invention or a novelty.
question: The patented 'new' Basmati variety was derived by:

options.A: Crossing Indian Basmati with semi-dwarf varieties and claiming it as a novel invention
options.D: Producing insulin chains in E. coli

explanation: The company crossed Indian farmers' Basmati with semi-dwarf types and claimed the result as a new invention.

source_sentence: The patent extends to functional equivalents, implying that other people selling Basmati rice could be restricted by the patent.
question: The Basmati patent controversy was serious because the patent:

options.A: Extended to functional equivalents, potentially restricting others from selling Basmati rice
options.C: Banned all rice cultivation in India
options.D: Required all diabetics to use animal insulin

explanation: Extension to functional equivalents meant the patent could restrict others from selling Basmati rice.

source_sentence: Several attempts have also been made to patent uses, products and processes based on Indian traditional herbal medicines, e.g., turmeric neem.
question: Examples of Indian traditional knowledge targeted by foreign patent attempts include:

options.A: Turmeric and neem
options.C: E. coli plasmids and retroviral vectors

explanation: Patent attempts have been made on turmeric, neem, and other traditional Indian herbal medicines.

source_sentence: The Indian Parliament has recently cleared the second amendment of the Indian Patents Bill, that takes such issues into consideration.
question: To address patent-related bioresource issues, the Indian Parliament:

options.A: Cleared the second amendment of the Indian Patents Bill

explanation: The second amendment of the Indian Patents Bill was cleared to address concerns about patents on traditional bio-resources.

source_sentence: Biopiracy is the term used to refer to the use of bio-resources by multinational companies and other organisations without proper authorisation from the countries and people concerned without compensatory payment.
question: Biopiracy refers to:

options.A: Use of bio-resources without proper authorisation or compensatory payment to concerned countries and people
options.B: Legal sharing of GM technology with farmers
options.C: Production of recombinant insulin in bacteria
options.D: Use of PCR for early HIV detection

explanation: Biopiracy is unauthorised commercial use of bio-resources without compensation to the source country or communities.

source_sentence: Most of the industrialised nations are rich financially but poor in biodiversity and traditional knowledge. In contrast the developing and the underdeveloped world is rich in biodiversity and traditional knowledge related to bio-resources.
question: Regarding biodiversity and traditional knowledge, industrialised nations are generally:

options.A: Financially rich but poor in biodiversity and traditional knowledge
options.B: Rich in both finances and biodiversity compared to all developing nations
options.D: The sole owners of all rice varieties worldwide

explanation: Industrialised nations tend to be financially wealthy but biodiversity-poor, unlike many developing countries.

source_sentence: Traditional knowledge related to bio-resources can be exploited to develop modern applications and can also be used to save time, effort and expenditure during their commercialisation.
question: Traditional knowledge related to bio-resources can help in commercialisation by:

options.A: Saving time, effort, and expenditure in developing modern applications
options.C: Eliminating the need for any patents globally

explanation: Traditional knowledge can guide development of modern applications and reduce commercialisation costs and time.

source_sentence: Therefore, some nations are developing laws to prevent such unauthorised exploitation of their bio-resources and traditional knowledge.
question: Some nations are developing laws to:

options.A: Prevent unauthorised exploitation of their bio-resources and traditional knowledge
options.D: Stop production of all recombinant therapeutics

explanation: Laws are being developed to protect bio-resources and traditional knowledge from unauthorised exploitation.

source_sentence: Techniques of tissue culture and somatic hybridisation offer vast potential for manipulation of plants in vitro to produce new varieties.
question: According to the chapter summary, tissue culture and somatic hybridisation:

options.A: Offer vast potential for in vitro plant manipulation to produce new varieties
options.C: Replace all need for gene therapy
options.D: Are used only for patent disputes

explanation: Tissue culture and somatic hybridisation enable extensive in vitro plant manipulation for new varieties.

source_sentence: Human insulin is made in bacteria yet its structure is absolutely identical to that of the natural molecule.
question: Recombinant human insulin produced in bacteria:

options.A: Has a structure absolutely identical to natural human insulin
options.B: Differs completely from natural insulin in sequence
options.C: Contains the C peptide in the final product
options.D: Always causes immune reactions unlike natural insulin

explanation: Bacterially produced recombinant human insulin is structurally identical to the natural hormone.

source_sentence: Viruses that attack their hosts and introduce their genetic material into the host cell as part of their replication cycle are used as vectors to transfer healthy genes.
question: In gene therapy, viruses are used as vectors because they:

options.A: Introduce their genetic material into host cells during their replication cycle
options.B: Produce Bt toxin in plant leaves
options.D: Are always destroyed before contacting cells

explanation: Viruses naturally deliver genetic material into host cells and are engineered as vectors for therapeutic genes.

source_sentence: The source of this complementary RNA could be from an infection by viruses having RNA genomes or mobile genetic elements (transposons) that replicate via an RNA intermediate.
question: In natural RNAi, the source of complementary RNA may be:

options.A: RNA viruses or transposons replicating via an RNA intermediate

explanation: Complementary RNA triggering RNAi may originate from RNA viruses or transposons that replicate through RNA.

source_sentence: Scientists have even isolated single cells from plants and after digesting their cell walls have been able to isolate naked protoplasts (surrounded by plasma membranes).
question: Plant protoplasts are:

options.A: Plant cells without cell walls, surrounded only by plasma membrane
options.D: Mature insulin A and B chains

explanation: Protoplasts are isolated plant cells whose walls have been removed, leaving the plasma membrane.

source_sentence: Well, this has been achieved – resulting in formation of tomato; unfortunately this plant did not have all the desired combination of characteristics for its commercial utilisation.
question: The tomato-potato somatic hybrid (often called 'tomato') failed commercially because:

options.A: It did not have all the desired combination of characteristics
options.C: It produced too much human insulin
options.D: It was immediately patented as Basmati

explanation: Although tomato-potato protoplast fusion was achieved, the hybrid lacked the full desired trait combination for commercial use.

source_sentence: By introducing genes from other species that alter the formation of this factor and studying the biological effects that result, information is obtained about the biological role of the factor in the body.
question: Introducing genes from other species to alter insulin-like growth factor formation in transgenic animals helps study:

options.A: The biological role of the factor in growth and development
options.C: Only Bt toxin activation in insect guts

explanation: Altering growth factor formation via transgenic approaches reveals the factor's biological role in the body.
